lead.text: *The practical infrastructure of being a functional adult in the modern world.*
Some of the most valuable skills of a modern life are the least glamorous: keeping documents in order, budgeting, planning travel, preparing for emergencies. This playbook is the checklist.

blocks.text: **THE TOOL — The 12 documents every adult should have organized**

Kept in a secure, encrypted, backed-up location that you can access from anywhere:
1. Passport (digital scan + printed backup)
2. National ID / driver's license
3. Birth certificate
4. Marriage / divorce documents if applicable
5. Bank details and account numbers
6. Insurance policies (health, home, auto, life)
7. Employment contract and pay stubs (last 12 months)
8. Tax returns (last 3 years)
9. Property documents (deed, lease, mortgage)
10. Medical records summary (allergies, medications, vaccinations)
11. Emergency contacts
12. Will and/or advance directives if applicable
Update annually. Notify one trusted person of the location and how to access.
A budget is not a moral instrument. It is a tool for knowing where your money is going and whether that matches what you actually value.

Every month, know four numbers:
• Income: what actually landed in your account.
• Fixed costs: rent/mortgage, utilities, insurance, subscriptions.
• Variable spending: everything else, categorized loosely (food, transport, personal, entertainment).
• Savings/investment: what actually got put away.
Notice: no rules, no moralism. Just visibility. Almost everyone who tracks these four numbers for three months makes a change to at least one — voluntarily, because the visibility itself changes behavior.

Regardless of destination:
• Passport with 6+ months validity.
• Emergency contacts saved offline.
• Bank's international assistance number saved.
• Photocopy of passport in checked bag; digital copies in encrypted cloud.
• Basic first aid: medications you need, electrolytes, bandages, tweezers.
• A small amount of local currency for arrivals.
• Universal adapter.
• Offline maps of your first 48 hours' destinations.
• Translation app with the language pack downloaded.
• A written itinerary shared with a trusted person at home.
For longer travel:
• Travel insurance.
• Notify banks of travel to prevent card blocks.
• Register with your country's embassy program if it exists.
You will not need it most of the time. When you need it, nothing else will do.

TIER 1 — 3 days
Water (1 gallon / 4L per person per day), non-perishable food, flashlight, batteries, first-aid kit, cash, phone charger, whistle, warm layer, important documents.
TIER 2 — 2 weeks
Extended food and water, cooking method that doesn't require utilities, sanitation supplies, any prescription medications, radio.
TIER 3 — extended disruption
Skills, community connections, savings, and health. The most valuable emergency resource is not stuff — it is relationships with capable neighbors.

• One password manager, one authenticator app.
• One cloud storage system with automated backup.
• One task manager. Not five apps you sometimes use.
• One calendar, shared appropriately.
• A yearly file structure that survives beyond any specific tool.
The specific tools will change. The habit of having one of each is what matters.

The single most valuable life skill is the willingness to try — and to fail — at things you haven't done before. Fix the broken lamp. Learn to cook one thing well. Change the tire once so you know you can. Read the insurance policy before you file the claim. Ask the question when you don't know.
This is the resourceful person, in ordinary life. Not heroic. Just capable.
*“Life capability is not glamorous. It is what separates the person who can handle a hard week from the person who can't.”*
